transcript.text: Bit of a weird one - my son put the microwave on for 10 minutes with nothing in it by accident. Now there's a horrible smell. Is it broken?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. It might be, and it needs checking before anyone uses it again. Running a microwave empty is one of the harder things you can do to it. With no food to soak up the microwave energy, it bounces around the cavity and back towards the part that makes it, the magnetron. Ten minutes is a long time for that. The most likely causes of the smell, in order:
1. The waveguide cover is scorched. This is the small flat panel on the inside wall, usually on the right, made of a card-like material called mica. It often burns or chars when a microwave runs empty, and that gives a strong, acrid smell.
2. The magnetron or the high-voltage parts behind the casing have overheated. That can leave a hot electrical or burning smell, and sometimes it means they're damaged.
3. Less likely: old food splatter inside got cooked hard and burnt off. That smells unpleasant but isn't harmful in itself. Please don't switch it on again, not even to test it. It needs a qualified engineer to look at it first, because the parts that may be damaged are inside the casing, where there are dangerous voltages even when it's unplugged. With it unplugged, these are safe things to look at. They'll help you describe it to an engineer:
1. Open the door and look at that small panel on the side wall. Burnt, blackened, bubbled or holed points strongly to the cover. Clean and intact makes the hidden parts more of a suspect.
2. Look round the cavity, roof and door for scorch marks, melted plastic or chipped paint. Any of those means heat damage inside the cooking space.
3. Notice where the smell is strongest. If it's mainly inside the cavity, that suggests the cover or burnt residue. If it's from the vents at the back or sides, that suggests the electrical parts behind the casing. On repair versus replacement: if it's an inexpensive microwave, a damaged magnetron often costs nearly as much to fix as a new one. A scorched waveguide cover on its own is usually a cheap repair. An engineer can tell you which it is. What do you see when you look at that side panel?

There's a brownish mark on the panel on the side wall. Also there was some smoke coming out of the vents at the side when I opened the door, and the smell is a hot electrical/burnt one. It's switched off at the switch but still plugged in - should I unplug it?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
If there are flames or smoke is still coming from it, keep away, don't open the door of an oven, microwave or dryer that is on fire, switch it off at the wall or the fuse box only if you can do that safely, get everyone out and call 999.
There's no fire, and the smoke was only at the time, when we stopped it. I just want to know if it's safe to go and unplug it at the wall now, and whether I should bin it.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes, it's safe to unplug it now. There's no fire, the smoke stopped when it was switched off, and it's been off since. With dry hands, switch the socket off if it has a switch, then pull the plug out by the plug body, not the cable. If the plug or socket feels hot, looks scorched or smells burnt, leave it and switch that circuit off at the fuse box instead. Then leave it unplugged. Should you bin it? Not necessarily, but don't use it again until an engineer has checked it. Putting together what you've told me, the brownish mark on the side panel, the smoke from the side vents and the hot electrical smell, here's my best reading: 1. Most likely, the magnetron or the high-voltage parts behind the casing overheated. Smoke from the side vents, rather than from inside the cooking space, points behind the casing. Those parts may or may not be damaged.
2. Also likely, the waveguide cover (that side panel) is scorched. Its brown mark is typical of a microwave run empty. On its own, that's usually a cheap fix. Only an engineer can tell which it is. The parts behind the casing can hold a dangerous charge even when it's unplugged, so please don't open it or test it yourself. On repair versus replacement:
• If it's an inexpensive freestanding microwave, replacing it is often the sensible choice. A damaged magnetron plus the call-out can cost close to the price of a new one.
• If it's a built-in or combination model, it's usually worth paying for an engineer's assessment first. It may turn out to be just the cover. Which kind is yours?

candidates: Waveguide (mica) cover scorched from running empty (high)
Magnetron or high-voltage parts overheated or damaged by running with no load (medium)
Old food splatter in the cavity cooked and burnt off (low)
